Project  Editors 

All  the  project  editors  on  the  staff  of  The  Encyclopedia 
of  Religion  wish  to  extend  their  thanks  to  the  board  of 
editors,  to  the  editorial  consultants,  and  to  the  contrib- 
utors to  this  work.  Our  gratitude  to  these  scholars  is 
beyond  measure.  The  following  project  editors  wish  to 
make  further,  personal  acknowledgments  of  special  as- 
sistance they  received  in  the  performance  of  their  du- 
ties. 

Paul  Bernabeo.  In  fulfilling  my  responsibilities  as 
associate  project  editor,  I  relied  heavily  and  continu- 
ously on  the  advice  and  support  of  the  encyclopedia's 
board  of  editors,  other  members  of  the  Macmillan  staff, 
and  numerous  outside  scholars,  colleagues,  and  friends. 
To  the  many  who  were  prevailed  upon — even  pes- 
tered— to  give  me  aid,  I  owe  my  sincere  thanks.  I  take 
pleasure,  too,  in  recalling  that  the  number  of  exceptions 
to  the  rule  of  friendly  cooperation  and  enthusiasm  evi- 
denced by  the  several  hundred  authors  with  whom  I 
had  the  honor  to  work  personally  during  the  years  of 
preparation  of  this  encyclopedia  is  so  small  as  to  be  al- 
most completely  forgotten. 


ACKNOWLEDGMENTS 


Plans  for  coverage  of  Christianity  originated  with 
Martin  E.  Marty  and  Richard  P.  McBrien.  Despite  con- 
flicting demands  on  their  time,  they  never  failed  in  their 
resolve  to  support  this  project  through  their  intellectual 
leadership,  reassuring  integrity,  and  good  will.  Profes- 
sor Marty  was  assisted  in  Chicago  by  Rehova  Arthur, 
Gwendolyn  Barnes,  Michelle  Harewood,  and  Judith 
Lawrence;  Professor  McBrien,  in  Notre  Dame,  by  San- 
dra Roman,  Donna  Shearer,  and  Kern  Trembath.  I  also 
wish  to  acknowledge  my  debt  for  guidance  in  the  area 
of  Eastern  Christianity  to  Stanley  Samuel  Harakas, 
John  Meyendorff,  A.  S.  Atiya,  and  my  staff  colleague 
Sirarpi  Feredjian-Aivazian.  Stephen  C.  Neill,  David  W. 
Lotz,  and  especially  Jaroslav  Pelikan  never  retracted 
their  generous  offers,  despite  my  frequent  exercising  of 
them,  to  provide  recommendations  of  authors  for  unas- 
signed  articles.  Beatrice  de  Bary,  Ronald  John  Zawilla, 
Kenneth  MacLeod,  and  Hans  Rollman  were  of  special 
help  with  particular  manuscripts  on  Christianity.  No 
two  people  more  than  Seth  E.  Kasten  and  John  M.  Cox, 
of  the  staff  of  the  Burke  Library,  Union  Theological 
Seminary,  New  York,  were  consulted  in  ways  that  ap- 
proached pestering;  their  patience  with  me  and  my  as- 
sistants was  great. 

Plans  for  coverage  of  African  religions  originated  with 
Victor  Turner.  Brainstorming  with  him  was  an  intellec- 
tual adventure  that  led  to  weeks  of  discerning  the  dif- 
fracted light  he  shed.  After  Victor  Turner's  death,  his 
wife,  Edith  Turner,  and  editorial  board  member  Law- 
rence E.  Sullivan  advised  and  supported  our  work  in 
this  area,  as  did  outside  specialists,  including  Benjamin 
C.  Ray,  John  Middleton,  Robert  M.  Baum,  John  M.  Jan- 
zen,  and  Wyatt  MacGaffey.  Thanks  are  also  due  Anne 
Robson  and  T.  E.  Faber  for  their  help  with  particular 
material  on  African  religions. 

Development  of  plans  for  coverage  of  philosophy  de- 
pended upon  Jacob  Needleman.  John  E.  Smith  and 
Wayne  Proudfoot  were  generous  benefactors  of  advice 
in  this  area  as  well. 

Plans  for  coverage  of  the  arts  originated  within  Mac- 
millan's  staff  under  the  nurturing  genius  of  the  senior 
project  editor,  Claude  Conyers.  Initial  advice  was  given 
by  Rosanne  Klass.  Subsequently,  many  specialists  were 
consulted  who  offered  valuable  help:  in  the  area  of  ar- 
chitecture, J.  G.  Davies;  in  iconography,  H.  G.  Kippen- 
berg,  Roger  Lipsey,  Richard  B.  Kowall,  and  Edward  J. 
Maloney;  in  music,  Johanna  Spector  and  Ter  Ellingson; 
in  drama  and  dance,  Richard  Schechner;  and  in  litera- 
ture, Nathan  A.  Scott,  Jr.,  and  Anthony  C.  Yu.  Thanks 
are  also  due  Renee  Renouf  for  her  assistance  with  par- 
ticular material  on  dance.  All  the  members  of  the  edi- 
torial board,  but  most  especially  Mircea  Eliade,  Joseph 
M.  Kitagawa,  and  Annemarie  Schimmel,  were  called 


upon  to  help  review  our  developing  coverage  of  the  arts 
and  religion.  This  they  did  graciously  despite  the  bur- 
den of  their  other  duties. 

Finally,  I  would  like  to  express  my  personal  gratitude 
to  my  assistants  who  not  only  provided  assistance  but 
who  also  brought  wisdom  and  intelligence  to  the  pro- 
ject. Thank  you,  once  again,  to  Nancy  G.  Wright,  who 
gave  shape  to  our  work  as  she  gave  it  and  me  support; 
to  W.  Cunningham  Bissell,  who  bravely  stopped  the 
gaps  in  my  knowledge  of  Africa;  to  Michael  Scott 
Cooper,  a  trouble-shooter  who  took  up  his  changing 
burdens  cheerfully  and  faithfully;  and  to  Richard  D. 
Hylton,  who  fought  a  good  fight  against  the  enigmas  of 
scholarly  language. 

Mark  D.  Cummings.  The  making  of  this  encyclope- 
dia has  been,  from  first  to  last,  a  collective  enterprise, 
engaging  a  community  of  scholars,  writers,  and  others 
who  generously  gave  of  their  skills  and  expertise  in  the 
finest  tradition  of  the  university.  As  the  staff  member 
responsible  for  our  coverage  of  Asian  religions,  I  owe 
first  and  foremost  a  deep  debt  of  gratitude  to  our  con- 
tributors, whose  efforts,  counsel,  and  ready  cooperation 
gave  life  and  shape  to  the  project,  and  to  the  members 
of  the  editorial  board,  whose  vision  and  persistence  are 
evident  on  every  page.  I  am  particularly  grateful  to  Jo- 
seph M.  Kitagawa,  whose  patience  and  erudition  did 
much  to  make  this  work  what  it  is,  and  whose  personal 
kindness  leaves  me  much  in  his  debt.  Professor  Kitaga- 
wa's  skill  in  conceptualizing  the  foundations  of  our  cov- 
erage, suggesting  contributors  for  various  entries,  and 
reviewing  the  products  of  their  labor,  lent  a  breadth 
and  consistency  to  the  whole  that  would  scarcely  have 
been  possible  otherwise.  Thanks  are  due  as  well  to  Wil- 
liam K.  Mahony  for  his  tireless  help  at  all  stages  of  the 
project,  and  especially  for  his  zealous  supervision  of  the 
materials  on  South  Asia.  Professor  Mahony  joins  me  in 
acknowledging  our  gratitude  to  Wendy  Doniger  O'Fla- 
herty  for  her  scholarly  concern  and  seemingly  bound- 
less good  will  for  the  project. 

It  is  also  my  great  pleasure  to  be  able  to  acknowledge 
here  my  indebtedness  to  a  small  group  of  individuals, 
some  close  friends,  others  known  to  me  only  as  corre- 
spondents, to  whom  I  was  able  to  turn  on  countless  oc- 
casions for  technical  advice,  help  in  planning  the  di- 
mensions of  articles,  recommendations  for  potential 
contributors,  evaluation  of  manuscripts,  or  administra- 
tive assistance.  These  include  Araki  Michio,  David  W. 
Chappell,  James  C.  Dobbins,  J.  Joseph  Errington,  Su-

Thurman,  Michael  L.  Walter,  Guy  R.  Welbon,  and  Stan- 
ley Weinstein.  For  his  erudition,  humanity,  and,  above 
all,  friendship,  I  owe  a  debt  of  gratitude  to  this  last  fig- 
ure that  cannot  adequately  be  expressed  here. 

No  one  who  was  not  involved  in  the  day-to-day  man- 
agement of  the  encyclopedia  can  begin  to  appreciate  the 
depth  of  commitment,  both  professional  and  personal, 
that  was  required  of  our  editorial  staff.  My  profound 
thanks,  then,  to  my  assistants,  scholars  all,  who  labored 
to  bring  this  project  to  fruition.  Constantina  Bailly  and 
Jeff  Edelstein  both  assumed  responsibility  for  major 
portions  of  the  materials  under  our  aegis — South  and 
Inner  Asia,  respectively — and  acquitted  their  responsi- 
bilities with  great  distinction.  To  their  efforts  much  of 
the  editorial  integrity  of  these  articles  is  due.  Ellen  Nes- 
kar  and  Gopal  Sukhu  labored  under  difficult  conditions 
with  our  materials  on  Chinese  religions  and  deserve 
credit  for  their  most  careful  reading  of  the  texts  with 
which  they  worked.  My  thanks  as  well  to  our  adminis- 
trative assistants,  Naella  Denby  and  Yasmin  Khan, 
both  of  whom  brought  grace  and  intelligence  to  every- 
thing they  did. 

Finally,  I  would  like  to  acknowledge  my  deepest  grat- 
itude to  Ann  K.  Burns,  whose  encouragement  and  self- 
lessness did  not  pass  unnoticed  in  the  years  it  took  to 
produce  this  work. 

Sirarpi  Feredjian-Aivazian.  As  an  early  member  of 
Macmillan's  editorial  staff  for  this  great  project,  I  was 
privileged  to  work  closely  with  three  members  of  the 
board  of  editors,  to  each  of  whom  a  friendly  note  of 
thanks  is  now  due.  Robert  M.  Seltzer  patiently  endured 
my  constant  queries  and  pleas  for  help  as  plans  were 
developed  and  manuscripts  were  received  on  the  reli- 
gions of  the  ancient  Near  East,  including  Israelite  reli- 
gion, and  on  Judaism.  Charles  J.  Adams  and  Annemarie 
Schimmel  cheerfully  responded  to  similar  queries  and 
pleas  concerning  articles  on  Islam.  To  all  three  I  extend 
my  gratitude. 

I  must  express  special  appreciation,  too,  to  several 
colleagues  on  the  Macmillan  staff  who  assumed  my  ed- 
itorial duties  upon  my  departure  for  maternity  leave. 
Sylvia  Juran  neatly  tied  up  all  loose  ends  in  the  ancient 
Near  East;  Stefanie  Siegmund  and  Edward  G.  Fram 
brought  their  considerable  expertise  to  bear  on  all  the 
manuscripts  concerning  Israelite  religion  and  Judaism; 
and  Miriam  Rosen  and  John  Wehba  polished  off  the  ar- 
ticles on  Islam  in  fine  style.  I  am  grateful  to  them  all 
for  their  successful  conclusion  of  work  that  I  had  so 
hopefully  begun. 

On  their  behalf,  I  am  glad  to  acknowledge  here  that 
credit  is  also  due  to  Leonard  H.  Lesko,  for  his  extraor- 
dinarily generous  help  on  Egyptian  religion;  to  Edward 
L.  Greenstein,  for  invaluable  aid  on  matters  pertaining 


to  the  Hebrew  scriptures;  and  to  Joan  S.  Friedman,  for 
conscientious  assistance  in  research  and  proofreading. 
Research  assistance  of  great  benefit  was  also  supplied 
by  Houssam  Khalil,  Middle  East  Section  of  the  Oriental 
Division,  New  York  Public  Library,  and  by  Merlye  Gas- 
ton, Near  East  Librarian,  Elmer  Holmes  Bobst  Library, 
New  York  University. 

Beverly  Moon.  My  work  on  the  encyclopedia  con- 
sisted of  monitoring  two  groups  of  articles:  essays  on 
Indo-European  religions  (with  the  exception  of  the  In- 
dian traditions,  which  were  planned  together  with  es- 
says on  other  Asian  religions)  and  a  group  of  articles 
dealing  with  religious  themes  and  concepts  from  the 
study  of  religion.  Mircea  Eliade  was  the  supervising  ed- 
itor of  both  units,  but  he  was  joined  by  nearly  all  the 
editors  in  planning  the  thematic  articles.  I  want  to 
thank  Joseph  M.  Kitagawa,  Annemarie  Schimmel,  and 
Charles  J.  Adams  for  their  kindness  in  answering  my 
many  calls  for  help  in  finding  contributors  and  in  re- 
viewing manuscripts.  Furthermore,  I  want  to  thank 
Lawrence  E.  Sullivan,  who  spent  a  summer  with  us  in 
New  York  finalizing  the  detailed  plans  for  the  unit  of 
thematic  articles.  This  was  a  time  of  tremendous  cre- 
ativity that  underlies  the  broad  coverage  that  the  unit 
achieves. 

One  of  Mircea  Eliade's  concerns  was  that  we  include 
articles  written  by  scholars  from  all  over  the  world  so 
that  the  encyclopedia  might  reflect  present-day  under- 
standings of  religion  in  a  complete  and  ecumenical  way. 
Many  of  the  articles  in  both  my  units  were  composed, 
therefore,  in  languages  other  than  English.  Translation 
of  these  articles  was  facilitated  by  the  superb  writing 
talent  of  David  Carpenter,  who  took  many  an  essay  and 
rendered  it  into  the  smoothest  English.  Staff  member 
Deborah  Sommer  shouldered  much  of  the  editing  and 
rewriting  of  articles,  in  addition  to  helping  me  discover 
the  most  efficient  ways  to  manage  an  immense  number 
of  manuscripts.  Katherine  Schulten,  my  administrative 
assistant,  consistently  and  cheerfully  assumed  many 
duties  of  the  editorial  process. 

The  articles  on  the  Greeks,  the  Romans,  the  Germans, 
and  so  on  were  more  easily  planned,  certainly,  than  ar- 
ticles on  topics  as  diverse  as  caves  and  ascension.  How- 
ever, they  were  not  always  easy  to  edit,  since  they 
raised  questions  of  consistency  in  the  transliteration  of 
numerous  languages.  Two  persons  were  especially  help- 
ful in  editing  these  pieces:  Gregory  D.  Alles  was  always 
willing  to  look  at  an  article  and  serve  as  reviewer  or 
editor,  and  our  senior  project  editor,  Claude  Conyers, 
jumped  in  at  the  eleventh  hour  to  lend  a  helping  hand. 

I  also  want  to  thank  the  many  scholars  to  whom  I 
turned  in  the  course  of  the  years  to  find  other  contribu- 
tors for  articles  on  every  imaginable  aspect  of  religious 


ACKNOWLEDGMENTS 


life.  Through  all  this  planning,  seeking  of  contributors, 
and  editing,  Professor  Eliade's  assistant,  Peter  C.  Chem- 
erv,  was  faithful  in  relaying  messages,  suggesting  solu- 
tions, and  giving  friendly  and  thoughtful  support. 

Most  of  all,  however,  I  would  like  to  express  my  deep- 
est gratitude  to  the  man  who  drew  me  into  the  history 
of  religions  in  the  first  place.  In  1966,  while  studying  at 
the  University  of  Chicago,  I  heard  two  other  students 
discussing  their  studies  with  Professor  Eliade.  At  that 
moment,  a  light  went  on  in  my  life  that  has  never  gone 
out.  I  matriculated  at  the  Divinity  School  and  started 
my  own  intellectual  odyssey.  Unfortunately,  I  had  to 
leave  Chicago  three  years  later,  and  so  it  was  a  real  re- 
turn to  find  myself  working  hand  in  hand  with  Mircea 
Eliade  on  this  great  project.  Memories  of  his  kindness 
and  generosity  will  be  with  me  always. 

James  Waller.  Coming  aboard  the  staff,  as  I  did, 
fairly  far  along  in  the  encyclopedia's  planning  process, 
I  owe  a  sizable  debt  of  gratitude  to  Charles  J.  Adams: 
by  the  time  of  my  arrival,  the  planning  of  our  coverage 
of  the  historical  and  contemporary  study  of  religion 
was,  because  of  his  work,  a  fait  accompli,  and  my  job 
was  made  much  easier  by  the  comprehensive  task  he 
had  performed.  Two  other  members  of  the  encyclope- 
dia's editorial  board  deserve  my  special  thanks.  First, 
Lawrence  E.  Sullivan,  on  whom  I  constantly  depended 
for  careful  review  of  articles  concerning  primal  tradi- 
tions and  without  whose  assistance  the  complex  job  of 
attempting  to  achieve  something  akin  to  editorial  uni- 
formity in  the  treatment  of  hundreds  of  local  traditions 
would  not  have  been  thinkable.  I  also  thank  William  K. 
Mahony  for  his  readiness  to  help  me  out  with  a  matter 
that  required  not  only  some  delicacy  but  also  a  chunk 
of  his  already  overburdened  schedule. 

I  am  likewise  grateful  to  several  of  the  encyclopedia's 
consultants  and  contributors.  Thanks  are  owed  espe- 
cially to  Pita  Kelekna,  without  whose  participation  our 
inspections  of  the  indigenous  religious  traditions  of 
South  America  would  be  much  less  varied;  to  Ronald 
M.  Berndt,  whose  masterful  hand  wove  our  coverage  of 
Australian  Aboriginal  religion;  and  to  Doris  M.  Heyden, 
whose  help  in  solving  problems  and  whose  enthusiasm 
for  our  project  were  boons,  and  with  whom  correspond- 
ing was  a  real  joy. 

Mention  is  due  to  a  number  of  people  whose  advice 
regarding  specific  difficulties  was  invaluable:  to  Louise 
Lamphere,  Emily  Sellon,  Peter  Sutton,  and  David  M. 
Wulff  I  express  my  wholehearted  thanks.  Thanks  ought 
also  to  be  sent  to  Marilyn  Hirsh,  who  graciously  lent 
her  talents  as  an  illustrator  to  our  project  (and  whose 


drawings  appear  in  the  articles  on  Buddhist  and  Hindu 
iconography),  and  to  John  M.  Cox,  who  suffered  in  l  lie 
way  only  a  good  friend  would  my  repeated  interrup- 
tions of  his  work. 

1  want  also  to  single  out  a  few  of  my  assistants  for 
praise  for  jobs  exceedingly  well  done.  Bibliographic  re- 
search is  not  the  sort  of  job  one  ordinarily  associates 
with  creativity;  however,  the  difficult  topography 
across  which  Bruno  Blumenfeld  was  forced,  by  the 
problems  with  which  I  presented  him,  to  discover  his 
way  continuously  pointed  up  his  brilliance  as  a  re- 
searcher (not  to  mention  his  semidivine  patience).  Dur- 
ing the  project's  final  months,  the  efficient,  sensitive 
copyediting  performed  by  Rita  M.  Campon  clarified 
much  that  had  been  murky,  and  Lucia  Lermond's  re- 
search and  rewriting  skills  enabled  us  to  put  a  number 
of  short — but  quite  troubled — articles  to  bed. 

Finally,  my  greatest  thanks  are  reserved  for  two  edi- 
torial assistants:  James  Noggle,  the  hiring  of  whom  was 
for  me  a  lucky  strike,  and  Mary  Edwardsen,  who  has 
several  times  in  our  lives  coupled  the  roles  of  collabo- 
rator and  friend,  and  with  whose  career  and  life  I  hope 
my  own  will  continue,  for  years  to  come,  to  be  en- 
twined. 


Collectively  as  associate  and  assistant  project  editors, 
we  take  pleasure  in  acknowledging  an  immense  debt  to 
the  two  members  of  the  staff  who — unlike  us — required 
no  instruction  in  how  to  make  an  encyclopedia.  After 
we  and  our  assistants  had  achieved  a  significant  pace  in 
our  editorial  journeys  through  the  various  regions  of  re- 
ligious studies,  many  of  us  converged  at  one  narrow 
pass.  The  expert  guide  at  that  pass  was  Karen  Ready, 
managing  editor  of  our  copy  department,  who  is  owed 
a  wealth  of  thanks  from  the  multitude  of  bustling  trav- 
elers who  sought  her  help.  She  never  failed  to  give  it 
freely,  judiciously,  and  cheerfully,  speeding  us  grate- 
fully on  our  way. 

Above  all,  however,  there  is  one  person  who  neglected 
no  detail  and  who  recognized  no  time  of  day,  day  of  the 
week,  or  season  of  the  year  but  as  a  time  to  work.  He 
shared  his  wisdom  generously,  spread  his  care  widely, 
and,  to  our  deep  and  enduring  admiration  and  respect, 
provided  the  perfect  example  of  one  who  could  indeed 
count  the  countless,  list  the  missing,  and  fix  the  unfix- 
able.  No  beacon  shone  more  powerfully  in  the  daily 
progress  of  our  work  than  his.  We  declare  sincerely 
and  affectionately  our  appreciation  of  the  gift  of 
apprenticeship  we  received  from  our  project's  senior 
editor,  Claude  Conyers.

Synoptic  Outline  of  Contents 


The  outline  presented  here  is  intended  to  provide  a  general  view  of  the  conceptual 
scheme  of  this  encyclopedia.  It  is  divided  into  two  parts:  The  Religions  and  The  His- 
tory of  Religion.  To  show  the  conceptual  components  of  the  encyclopedia's  coverage, 
each  of  these  general  parts  is  subdivided  into  a  variety  of  sections.  Because  the  rubrics 
used  as  section  headings  are  not  necessarily  mutually  exclusive,  certain  entries  in  the 
encyclopedia  are  listed  in  more  than  one  section. 


I 

THE   RELIGIONS 

Part  I  of  this  outline  presents  the  encyclopedia' s  coverage  of  the  diversity  of  religious 
traditions  organized  according  to  historical,  geographical,  and  ethnographic  continu- 
ities. It  is  arranged  in  forty-four  sections:

Afro-American  Religions

Arctic  Religions

II 

THE   HISTORY  OF  RELIGION 

Part  II  of  this  outline  presents  the  encyclopedia  s  coverage  of  religion  as  a  universal 
phenomenon.  It  is  organized  according  to  the  following  scheme: 

Religious  Phenomena 
Art,  Science,  and  Society 

Art  and  Religion 
Science  and  Religion 
Society  and  Religion 
The  Study  of  Religion 
History  of  Study 
Methods  of  Study 
Philosophy  and  Religion 
Scholarly  Terms 
Scholars  of  Religion 

In  the  first  two  sections,  Religious  Phenomena  and  Art,  Science,  and  Society,  are 
listed  entries  that  present  the  fruits  of  the  scholarly  study  of  religion.  In  the  third  sec- 
tion, The  Study  of  Religion,  are  listed  entries  that  focus  attention  on  the  history  and 
techniques  of  religious  studies  themselves. 

Religious  Phenomena 

Here  are  listed  entries  that  concern  objects,  symbols,  practices,  beliefs,  themes,  and 
motifs  that  are  observable  transreligionally,  that  is,  as  elements  of  more  than  one 
religious  tradition.  Typically,  an  entry  listed  here  specifies  a  phenomenon  that  members 
of  various  religious  traditions  would  recognize  as  a  component  of  religious  life.

Kingdom  of  God.     In  volume  8,  page  311,  following  line 

1 7  from  the  foot  of  column  a,  insert  the  following  three 

paragraphs: 

The  popular  piety  of  hymnody.  Even  for  Luther,  when 
he  turned  hymn-writer,  the  only  opposite  to  God's  king- 
dom can  be  Satan's:  in  Ein  feste  Burg  (1529)  God's  op- 
posite is  the  "Prince  of  this  world"  (John  12:31),  and  the 
sole  kingdom  is  the  one  we  inherit,  Das  Reich  muss  uns 
doch  bleiben.  The  masters  of  English  hymnody,  who  al- 
ways attribute  the  kingdom  to  Jesus,  suffuse  it  with  the 
social  witness  of  the  Evangelical  revival.  Thus  Isaac 
Watts  in  his  paraphrase  (1719)  of  the  messianic  Psalm 
72:  "Jesus  shall  reign  where'er  the  sun  .  .  .  his  kingdom 
stretch  from  shore  to  shore."  Charles  Wesley's  Christ- 
mas hymn  (1739)  once  began  "Glory  to  the  King  of 
kings!";  congregations  still  sing,  "Hail,  the  Sun  of  Righ- 
teousness! /  Hail,  the  heav'n-born  Prince  of  Peace!" 
Their  focus  on  the  person  of  Jesus  is  especially  plain  in 
their  transformation  of  the  "kingship  Psalms":  Watts's 
Christmas  hymn  (1719)  "Joy  to  the  world!  the  Lord  is 
come;  /  Let  earth  receive  her  King"  adapts  Psalm  98; 
Charles  Wesley's  Ascension  hymn  "Hail  the  day  that 
sees  him  rise  .  .  .  Take  the  King  of  Glory  in!"  reworks 
Psalm  24. 

Puritanism  and  the  Social  Gospel.  English  Puritans 
commonly  speak  of  God  as  king.  In  his  A  Holy  Common- 
wealth (1659),  Richard  Baxter  affirms  that  "the  world  is 
a  Kingdom  whereof  God  is  the  King  ...  an  absolute 
Monarchy.  ...  All  men  are  the  subjects  of  God's  king- 
dom" (Richard  Niebuhr,  1937,  p.  52).  It  is  a  false  boast 
when  in  John  Milton's  Paradise  Lost  Satan  claims  "Di- 
vided Empire  with  Heaven's  King  I  hold"  (4.111).  In 
America,  where  the  symbolism  of  monarchy  was  less 
apt,  the  emphasis  merely  shifts  to  the  kingdom  of  God. 
Jonathan  Edwards  in  his  History  of  Redemption  regards 
the  kingdom  of  heaven  upon  earth  as  a  prosperous  age 
of  the  church  before  the  apostasy  and  last  judgment. 
The    Puritan    inheritance    was    secularized    in    Walter 


Rauschenbusch's  notion  of  the  Social  Gospel,  in  which 
the  realization  of  the  kingdom  is  identified  with  histor- 
ical progress.  In  a  manuscript  of  about  1891,  posthu- 
mously published  as  The  Righteousness  of  the  Kingdom 
(Nashville,  1968),  Rauschenbusch  holds  that  the  "pro- 
gram of  the  Christian  revolution,"  namely,  the  kingdom 
of  God  on  earth,  "includes  a  twofold  aim:  the  regenera- 
tion of  every  individual  to  divine  sonship  and  eternal 
life,  and  the  victory  of  the  spirit  of  Christ  over  the  spirit 
of  this  world  in  .  .  .  all  the  institutions  formed  by  hu- 
man society"  (p.  110). 

The  theology  of  the  future.  After  the  reaction  to  nine- 
teenth-century liberal  theology  in  Bultmann's  existen- 
tialism and  Barth's  neoorthodoxy,  the  1960s  saw  new 
theologies  that  were  oriented  toward  the  future.  For  ex- 
ample, Wolfhart  Pannenberg  in  his  Theology  and  the 
Kingdom  of  God  (Philadelphia,  1969)  writes:  "If  the 
Kingdom  of  God  and  the  mode  of  his  existence  (power 
and  being)  belong  together,  then  the  message  of  the 
coming  kingdom  implies  that  God  in  his  very  being  is 
the  future  of  the  world"  (p.  61).  And  Jiirgen  Moltmann 
in  his  Theology  of  Hope  (trans.  J.  W.  Weitch,  London, 
1967)  holds  that  "the  kingdom  is  present  here  as  prom- 
ise and  hope  for  the  future  horizon  of  all  things"  (p. 
223). 

Unitarian  Universalist  Association.     In  volume  15,  page 
144,  line  18  from  the  foot  of  column  b,  insert  text,  to 
read  as  follows: 
of  the   Dissenters'  Chapels  Act  (1844),  which  assured 
Unitarians  of  their  churches. 

James  Martineau  (1805-1900),  who  exercised  great 
influence  among  English  Unitarians,  challenged  Priest- 
ley's theology  with  his  emphases  on  ethics  and  intui- 
tion. Martineau,  who  desired  comprehension  in  a  na- 
tional liberal  church,  preferred  the  name  Free  Christian 
to  Unitarian.  In  1928,  English  Unitarian  denomination- 
alists  and  those  who  were  influenced  by  Martineau's

Free  Christian  views  united  to  form  the  General  Assem- 
bly of  Unitarian  and  Free  Christian  Churches.  The  Non- 
Subscribing  Presbyterian  Church  of  Ireland,  which  de- 
rives from  the  influence  of  Thomas  Emlyn  (1663-1741), 
and  some  Welsh  and  Scottish  churches,  are  different 
expressions  of  English  Unitarianism. 

American  Unitarianism  gradually  emerged  during  the 
eighteenth  century  within  Congregationalism,  largely  be- 


cause of  the  influence  of  Arminian  theology,  which 
stressed  the  human  capacity  to  respond  to  grace,  and  Ar- 
ian  Christology.  This  gradual  development  resulted  in 
conflicts  that  culminated  in  the  appointment  of  a  liberal, 
Henry  Ware,  as  Hollis  Professor  of  Divinity  at  Harvard 
College  in  1805.  The  liberals  were  accused  of  covertly 
agreeing  with  Belsham's  humanitarian  Christology.
